items.title: William Russell Interview, 1976-02-16
items.q: I use as an example the Eddie Condon bunch... they'll be insulted... I blame it just to say the Eddie Conlon group in some respects were that way.

ctx.x: Wouldn't that depend on where they were playing, though?

Yeah, that's it. But if I should say in a dance hall where they should play just good dance music, and not, there again, maybe unjustly, I use as an example the Eddie Condon bunch, say the bunch of Knicks, or say Jazz Limited in Chicago, where if you request something that isn't the so-called Dixieland number, well, they'll be insulted, you know, if you'd ask them to play some late popular tune. Well, no, that's not one of our numbers. In other words, they consider themselves as artists, and they're playing in…
It seems to me that the New Orleans style music depended very importantly on having a certain mood, that one had to be in a good mood. You couldn't decide to say, forget it.

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1962-08-31
items.q: say the usual ones that used to play at Nick's or Eddie Conlon's. I don't mean Eddie Conlon, he's a very good talker and quite a friendly guy, but I mean the type of musicians...

ctx.x: You want to talk about some of these musicians you've encountered in the course of your career now?

Yes, I might talk a little bit. I happened to pick up an old big box at home I have called Notes, and I dug out a few of the notebooks and other things. One package of notes envelope called Jazzmen material that we collected in 1938 when we were working on Jazzmen. Unfortunately then, we not only didn't have tape recording, we didn't have any other recorders. Nobody was hardly recording interviews.
